sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: To set dhikr reminders on iPhone, stack three layers: an ayah on your Lock Screen that you see all day, a few timed Reminders for morning and evening adhkar, and a Focus mode for prayer times. QuranWall covers the first layer, putting an ayah on your Lock Screen wallpaper and Home Screen widget.

sections.text: You never forget to check your phone. You forget to remember Allah — not from a lack of love, but because the day is loud and the screen is louder. If you have searched **how to set dhikr reminders iphone** guides before, you know the trap: notifications get swiped away and good intentions fade by Tuesday. Most people typing **how to set dhikr reminders iphone** into Google want one outcome — more remembrance, less willpower. This guide gives you three layers that deliver exactly that.

Here is the uncomfortable math. You pick up your phone many times a day, and each one is a moment your attention is already on the glass. The question is not whether you will look — it is what meets you when you do. A dhikr reminder works when it rides on a habit you already have, instead of asking for a brand-new one. That is also why a [Quran verse on your lock screen](/blog/quran-verse-iphone-lock-screen) tends to outlast a counter app you have to remember to open.
Method 1: Put remembrance where you already look

The most durable answer to **how to set dhikr reminders iphone** is to stop thinking in notifications and start thinking in surfaces. Your lock screen is the surface you see before any app or feed. Place a short dhikr or ayah there — *SubhanAllah*, *Alhamdulillah*, a line of the Quran — and remembrance becomes passive. You do not have to act; you simply read what is already in front of you. QuranWall covers the ayah half of this idea: it carries a verse onto the most-seen surface of your phone, and the widget can show a new ayah every day if you turn on auto-rotate, so it doesn't go stale. If you are still choosing an app, see our [best dhikr app for iPhone](/blog/best-dhikr-app-for-iphone) ranking.

sections.content: Pair the verse with one short dhikr you are working on this month. Seeing *Astaghfirullah* fifty times a day does more than a single buzzing reminder ever will.

sections.text: Method 2: Set time-based dhikr reminders in iOS

For morning and evening adhkar, a scheduled nudge genuinely helps. The built-in Reminders app can fire at a set time on a daily repeat, so the after-Fajr and after-Maghrib windows never slip by unnoticed. Keep the wording specific — *Morning adhkar*, not just *dhikr* — so the cue tells you exactly what to do.

items: Open the **Reminders** app and create a new list called **Adhkar**.
Add a reminder such as *Morning adhkar* and tap the **info (i)** button.
Turn on **At a Time**, set it just after your Fajr window, and choose **Repeat > Daily**.
Add a second reminder for evening adhkar after Maghrib, on the same daily repeat.
Optionally tap **At a Location** so a dua reminder fires when you leave home.

sections.content: Keep timed reminders few. Two or three a day get honored; ten a day get ignored — and then switched off entirely.

sections.text: Method 3: Anchor dhikr to a Focus mode

A Focus mode quiets the noise and can swap your lock screen at set times (lock screens linked to a Focus need iOS 16 or later) — ideal for tying remembrance to salah. Build a Prayer or Quiet Time Focus that hides distracting apps and shows a dhikr wallpaper during prayer windows. The full walkthrough lives in our guide to setting up a [Quran Focus mode on iPhone](/blog/quran-focus-mode-iphone). For a whole morning built around it, see our [Muslim morning routine on iPhone](/blog/muslim-morning-routine-iphone) setup.
Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured.

Two things quietly break every dhikr-reminder setup. The first is fatigue: a notification you have seen a hundred times turns invisible, and you start swiping it away without reading a word. The second is upkeep — re-making and re-setting a dhikr wallpaper image is its own small chore, and by week two you have stopped. That is the whole trick to **how to set dhikr reminders iphone** that survive: lean on the passive lock-screen layer, and make changing the words as light as you can. QuranWall handles that for the verse: you pick the ayah in the app and it takes a few taps, with no image to make, and the widget can show a new ayah every day if you turn on auto-rotate.

items: **Stack, do not scatter.** One passive lock-screen layer plus two timed reminders beats a dozen notifications.
**Tie each cue to an existing habit** — after a prayer, on every unlock, when you walk out the door.
**Rotate the words** so they never fade into the background. Fresh text gets read; stale text gets ignored.
**Start small.** One dhikr you actually notice is worth more than a perfect system you abandon.
